turns.user: sanity check, i ran git pull and it said 'error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by merge: src/app.js'. so i did git stash, then git pull, then git stash pop. thats the right move right
turns.assistant:
Yes, that's a standard and safe way to handle it.

Git refused the pull because it would overwrite uncommitted changes in src/app.js. Stashing set those changes aside, the pull brought in the remote commits, and stash pop reapplies your changes on top.

One thing to watch: if stash pop reports a conflict in src/app.js, the file will have conflict markers. Resolve them, git add the file, and then git stash drop to remove the stash entry. If you prefer a single command next time, git pull --autostash does the same thing in one step.

turns.user: building a small expense tracker for me and my partner, need a database. comparing postgres, mysql and sqlite. we dont need multi user writes, just the two of us, prob under 100k rows. which one should i use
turns.assistant:
For that use case, SQLite is the best fit. It's a single file, there's nothing to install or run, and it handles 100,000 rows easily. It also handles two people fine as long as you aren't writing at the same time very often, which you won't be with an expense tracker.

Postgres is the most capable of the three, and it's the right choice if you want features like strong concurrency or complex JSON handling. For a two-person app it's more setup than you need.

MySQL is also fine, but it doesn't give you anything over SQLite for this, and you'd have to run a server.

Start with SQLite and keep your queries standard SQL, so you can move to Postgres later if you need to.

turns.user: we might want to put it on a server later and have it on my phone too. does that change it
turns.assistant:
It might change the answer a little, but not much. The phone part mostly depends on how the app is built, not the database. A simple way is to host the app on a small server and use the browser or a mobile app to connect.

If you do that, you have two reasonable options:

- Keep SQLite on the server. It's still fine for two users, and you can back up the file with a cron job or a tool like Litestream.
- Move to Postgres, probably on a managed service. It costs more, but it's more robust if the app grows or you add more users later.

For now, SQLite still makes sense. Keep the data access in one layer of code so switching later is a small job.

turns.user: sanity check, i have 3 cards. 4200 at 24.9%, 1800 at 19.5%, 900 at 0% (promo ending in march). im paying 350 a month total. i want to pay the highest interest first (avalanche) thats the right call
turns.assistant:
Yes, avalanche is the right approach for minimizing total interest. Pay the minimum on the other two cards and put the rest of your 350 toward the 24.9% card.

The 0% card is the one to watch. When the promo ends in March, the rate will jump, and it might be higher than 19.5%. Before March, check what the rate will become. If it's higher than the 24.9% card's rate, it becomes the top priority, and you'd switch the avalanche target at that point.

Your monthly interest on the 24.9% card is roughly 4,200 × 24.9% / 12, about $87, so paying a bit more toward it each month saves real money.

turns.user: what if i get a 0% balance transfer card for 18 months, should i move the 4200 there
turns.assistant:
It can be a good move, but check a few numbers first:

- Balance transfer fees are usually 3 to 5 percent. On 4,200, that's $126 to $210 upfront.
- To clear it within the 18 months, you'd need about $233 a month toward that balance alone. You're already paying $350 across everything, so it's doable if your budget allows it.
- Check the transfer limit. The new card might not approve the full $4,200.
- Don't put new purchases on the new card, since those often get a higher rate.
- Set a reminder for a few months before the promo ends, so you know what the rate will be if you still have a balance.

If the fee is paid and you clear the balance in time, you'll save far more interest than you pay in fees.

turns.user: i keep failing my protein goal, im stuck at like 60g most days and the goal is 120. i tried shakes and they made me bloated. i need ideas that arent just chicken breast every day, im so sick of it. i eat out for lunch a lot so that part is hard
turns.assistant:
Hitting 120 g by eating out is harder, but it's doable with a few swaps and some planning around the restaurant meals.

Ideas that don't rely on chicken breast:

- Eggs and egg whites: a 3-egg scramble at breakfast is about 19 g.
- Greek yogurt or skyr, if you tolerate dairy: about 20 g per 200 g pot.
- Fish, like canned tuna or salmon: a tin of tuna is around 25 g.
- Lean beef or pork: sirloin, pork tenderloin, or lean mince.
- Tofu, tempeh or seitan for a plant-based option.
- Cottage cheese, which is high in protein and easy to add as a snack.

When you're eating out, look for a grilled protein you can add as a side, like a grilled fish or steak portion, or ask for extra protein on a bowl. Most fast-casual places will add it for a small charge.

- Lactose-free Greek-style yogurt or lactose-free skyr. Many brands have the same protein content as regular.
- Lactose-free cottage cheese.
- Tofu, which can go in a stir-fry, a scramble, or a bowl.

turns.user: ugh, my H-1B stamping appointment in Toronto got cancelled and they rebooked me 4 months out. i need to start a project in Seattle in January and my employer is stressing. any ideas for getting an earlier appointment, or a different city?
turns.assistant:
A few options to try, in roughly this order:

- Check the appointment system often, every day if you can. Cancelled slots reappear, and they're often taken within hours.
- Ask your employer's immigration lawyer whether an expedited appointment request is possible. These are usually for urgent cases, such as needing to travel for work soon, and they need supporting documents from your employer.
- Check whether you're eligible to apply at another consulate. Rules for this depend on your nationality and where you live, so confirm the current policy on the State Department website before you book anything.
- Look at whether a different category of visa applies, if your situation changed. This is a question for your immigration lawyer, not something to change on your own.

If you do get an expedited slot, have your employer letter and project details ready, since the consulate may ask for them.

turns.user: the lawyer said the expedite request needs proof the project is starting in january, do i have an offer letter for that or does it need to be something else
turns.assistant:
An offer letter or employment letter is usually the core document, but for an expedite request the consulate typically wants proof that the travel or start date is firm. Good options are:

- A letter from your employer on company letterhead that states your position, your start date or project start, and the location in Seattle.
- A copy of the project or assignment letter, if your company issues one.
- An email from your manager confirming the January start, which is a reasonable backup.

Your lawyer will know exactly what the consulate accepts for the current process, so ask them to confirm the list before you submit. Make sure every date in the documents matches your application and your travel plans.
